title: Density — why a kilogram of feathers takes up so much more space
examTip: Always check your units. Examiners may give mass in grams and volume in cm³. They may want the answer in kg/m³. Know how to convert: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
introTips: A kilogram of feathers and a kilogram of iron have the same mass. But the feathers fill a room, and the iron fits in your hand.
Density is why steel ships can float. It is the shape and what is inside that matters, not just the material.
This topic links straight to the required practical. You will measure density in the lab.
intro: Why does wood float while a nail sinks, even if the nail is lighter? Why is a bag of flour much heavier than the same size bag of popcorn? The answer is density. Density measures how much mass is packed into a given volume. It is one of the most useful quantities in science. It tells you what things are made of. It predicts whether they will float. The particle model explains well why different substances have different densities.

basics.text: Mass is how much stuff an object is made of. It is measured in kilograms (kg). A full suitcase has more mass than an empty one.
Volume is how much space something takes up. It is measured in cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³). A cube 1 cm along each side has a volume of 1 cm³.
1 kg is 1000 g. A cube 1 metre along each side is 1 m³, and it holds 1,000,000 cm³.
Everything is made of tiny particles, far too small to see. They are always moving. In a hotter object they move faster.
Put things in water and some float while others sink. A wooden block floats. A stone sinks.
Letters in an equation stand for quantities, such as t for time. Two letters written side by side are multiplied together. To use it, swap the letters for numbers.

keyPoints.heading: What density is and why it matters
keyPoints.content: Density measures how much mass is packed into a given volume. The equation is: ρ = m / V Where: ρ = density (kg/m³ or g/cm³), m = mass (kg or g), V = volume (m³ or cm³) A substance with high density has particles that are heavier, more closely packed, or both. Some key densities: - Air: ~1.2 kg/m³ - Water: 1000 kg/m³ (1 g/cm³) - Aluminium: 2700 kg/m³ - Iron: 7900 kg/m³ - Gold: 19,300 kg/m³ Floating and sinking: compare the object with the fluid it is in. An object floats if it is less dense than the fluid. An object sinks if it is denser than the fluid.
writeBullets: Density (ρ) = mass (m) ÷ volume (V). Unit: kg/m³ or g/cm³
High density — particles are heavier, more closely packed, or both
Water: 1000 kg/m³; Air: ~1.2 kg/m³; Iron: 7900 kg/m³; Gold: 19,300 kg/m³
An object floats if density < fluid density. It sinks if density > fluid density

keyTerms.def: Mass per unit volume — how much mass is packed into a given space. Symbol: ρ (rho). Unit: kg/m³
The density equation: density equals mass divided by volume

keyPoints.memTip: ρ = m/V. Think 'rho equals mass over volume'. Rearrange using the triangle: cover what you want, and the rest is the calculation.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to mix up mass and density. A large object can have low density, like a balloon. A small object can have high density, like a lead weight.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating density — worked examples
keyPoints.content: The density equation and its rearrangements: ρ = m/V   m = ρV   V = m/ρ Worked example 1 — will it float? A block of pine wood has mass 600 g and volume 1000 cm³. ρ = m/V = 600/1000 = 0.6 g/cm³ = 600 kg/m³ 600 kg/m³ < 1000 kg/m³ (water), so the wood floats. ✓ Worked example 2 — finding mass from density and volume A gold ring has volume 0.8 cm³. Density of gold = 19.3 g/cm³. m = ρV = 19.3 × 0.8 = 15.4 g Worked example 3 — unit conversion A substance has density 2.7 g/cm³. Convert to kg/m³. 2.7 g/cm³ × 1000 = 2700 kg/m³ (aluminium) Worked example 4 — a change of state When a substance changes state, its mass stays the same. Its volume can change, so its density changes. A 2.7 kg block of a solid has a volume of 0.001 m³. Its density is 2.7 ÷ 0.001 = 2700 kg/m³. The block melts. The liquid still has a mass of 2.7 kg, but its volume is 0.00108 m³. ρ = m/V = 2.7 ÷ 0.00108 = 2500 kg/m³. Same mass, bigger volume, lower density. Unit conversion rule: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ To convert g/cm³ → kg/m³: multiply by 1000 To convert kg/m³ → g/cm³: divide by 1000
writeBullets: ρ = m/V. It rearranges to m = ρV and V = m/ρ
Always check units. Use the same units all through a calculation
1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Multiply by 1000 to convert g/cm³ to kg/m³
Mass is conserved in a change of state. If the volume changes, the density changes
To check floating, compare the density you worked out with the density of the fluid
If density < fluid density → floats. If density > fluid density → sinks

keyTerms.def: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Multiply by 1000 to convert g/cm³ to kg/m³

keyPoints.memTip: Use a formula triangle. Put ρ at the top, and m and V at the bottom. Cover what you want to find.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Unit conversion errors lose the most marks in density questions. Practise them on purpose.

keyPoints.heading: Measuring density in the lab (required practical)
keyPoints.content: There are three set-ups you need to know for the required practical: 1. Regular solid (e.g., cuboid or cylinder): - Measure its size with a ruler. For a cuboid: length, width and height. For a cylinder: radius and height - For small objects, use a micrometer or Vernier callipers. They measure small lengths more precisely than a ruler - Work out the volume with a formula: V = l × w × h (cuboid) or V = πr²h (cylinder) - Measure the mass using a balance - Calculate: ρ = m/V 2. Irregular solid (e.g., a stone or lump of metal): - Measure the mass with a balance - Fill a eureka can (displacement can) with water up to the spout. Then lower the object in gently - Collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder. The volume of water displaced = the volume of the object - Or use a measuring cylinder. Record the water level, add the object, and record the new level. Subtract to find the volume - Calculate: ρ = m/V 3. Liquids: - Measure a known volume of liquid using a measuring cylinder - Measure the mass of the empty container, then with the liquid. Subtract to find the mass of the liquid alone - Calculate: ρ = m/V Sources of error: parallax error when reading the measuring cylinder. Not fully covering the object with water. Using a worn ruler.
writeBullets: Regular solid — measure its size with a ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers. Use a formula for the volume. Use a balance for mass
Irregular solid — find the volume by displacement, with a eureka can or measuring cylinder
Volume of displaced water = volume of the irregular object
Liquid — measure a known volume with a measuring cylinder. Find its mass with a balance
All methods: measure mass and volume separately, then use ρ = m/V
Sources of error: parallax, not fully covering the object, worn equipment

keyTerms.def: A displacement can filled to the brim — used to measure the volume of an irregular object by collecting the water it displaces
The volume of liquid pushed aside when an object is submerged — equals the volume of the object

keyPoints.memTip: Regular → ruler (or micrometer, Vernier callipers) and formula. Irregular → water displacement.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Exam questions often ask you to describe the method for an irregular object. Make sure you say you collect the displaced water, not just 'put it in water'.

keyPoints.heading: Density and states of matter
keyPoints.content: The particle model explains why the three states of matter have such different densities: Gases are far less dense than liquids and solids. This is because the particles are very far apart. Most of a gas is empty space. For example, air (~1.2 kg/m³) is about 800 times less dense than water (1000 kg/m³). In a liquid, the particles are still close together, but not in a regular pattern. So liquids and solids have similar densities. Both are far denser than gases. Solids are usually denser than liquids of the same substance. This is because particles in a solid are packed more tightly. Comparing states: - Aluminium solid: 2700 kg/m³ - Aluminium vapour: far less dense (particles very spread out) The density of a liquid compared with its gas is typically about 1000:1.
writeBullets: Gases are far less dense than solids and liquids. They are mostly empty space between particles
Liquid particles are close together, but not in a regular pattern. So liquid and solid densities are similar
Solids are usually denser than liquids of the same substance. Their particles are packed more tightly
Liquid to gas density ratio: typically ~1000:1

keyTerms.def: How close together and how regular the particles are. It explains the density of each state

keyPoints.memTip: Gas: particles far apart, low density. Liquid and solid: particles close together, high density.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Explain density differences using the particles. Say how close together they are in each state, not just the numbers.

0.question: Block A and block B have the same volume. Block A has twice the mass. What can you say about their densities?
options: Block A has twice the density of block B
Block B has twice the density of block A
You cannot tell without knowing what they are made of
0.correctFeedback: Correct. ρ = m/V. Same volume and twice the mass means twice the density.
0.wrongFeedback: Density is mass per unit volume. The volumes are the same, so the block with more mass is denser. Twice the mass gives twice the density.

1.question: A metal has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is its density in kg/m³?
1.wrongFeedback: To convert g/cm³ to kg/m³, multiply by 1000. So 2.7 g/cm³ = 2700 kg/m³.

2.question: How would you measure the volume of an irregular lump of rock in the lab?
options: Put it in water in a eureka can or measuring cylinder. Measure the volume of water displaced
Measure its length, width and height with a ruler and multiply them together
Weigh it on a balance and divide by its known density
Place it on a measuring cylinder and read off the scale
2.correctFeedback: Spot on. For irregular objects you use water displacement. The volume of water pushed out equals the volume of the object.
2.wrongFeedback: You can only use length × width × height for regular shapes like cuboids. For irregular shapes, use water displacement. Collect the water from a eureka can in a measuring cylinder. Or read the rise in water level in a measuring cylinder.

3.question: Why is a gas much less dense than the same substance as a liquid?
options: Its particles are much further apart, so the same mass takes up much more volume
A gas has fewer particles in each kilogram
3.correctFeedback: Right. The particles are the same. In a gas they are far apart, so the same mass fills a much bigger volume.
3.wrongFeedback: A change of state does not change the particles or their mass. In a gas the particles are far apart. The same mass takes up far more volume, so the density is much lower.

commonMistakes: Dividing volume by mass instead of mass by volume. Remember ρ = m/V, not V/m.
Forgetting to convert units. Mixing grams with m³, or cm³ with kg, gives nonsense answers. Use the same units all the way through.
Saying an object 'loses mass' when placed in water. It doesn't. A fully submerged object displaces its own volume of water, not its own mass.
Forgetting to subtract the empty container's mass when finding a liquid's density.
examTips: In every density calculation, clearly show your formula, substitution and units. The mark scheme gives marks for each step.
If asked whether an object floats or sinks, work out its density. Compare it directly with the fluid's density, and say so clearly.
For the required practical, know the method for BOTH regular and irregular objects. Say which instrument measures which quantity.
revisionCardBullets: Density equation: ρ = m/V (rho = mass ÷ volume)
Units: kg/m³ or g/cm³. Conversion: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³
Water: 1000 kg/m³ (1 g/cm³). This is the key density to compare with
An object floats if density < fluid density. It sinks if density > fluid density
Regular solid: measure its size with a ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers → work out the volume with a formula
Irregular solid: use displacement in a eureka can or measuring cylinder
Volume of displaced water = volume of submerged object
Liquid: use measuring cylinder for volume, balance for mass
Gases are far less dense than liquids and solids. They are mostly empty space
Always use the same units and show every step in calculations
